newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia gets more taxes, spending cuts loom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia gets more taxes, spending cuts loom.

text.p: Russia raked in more taxes in April than in any of the previous 18 months, but officials promised on Wednesday to press ahead with plans to cut spending across the board to alleviate budgetary pressures.
An official from the state tax service said revenues were 20.1 trillion roubles ($3.5 billion) in April, or 25 percent more than the monthly average for the first quarter.
This was the highest monthly figure for 18 months, but it was still only 80 percent of planned levels, which means the government must press ahead and cut, or sequester, spending.
Under the budget law parliament must approve plans for sequestration if revenues are less than 90 percent of plan.
First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin said Russia wanted to bring 1997 spending down to 15.6 percent of gross domestic product, from 19.4 percent in the original budget.
Parliament, dominated by communists and their allies, is due to discuss the changes next week, but deputies have already served notice that they will oppose the plans.

Communist deputy Viktor Ilyukhin wants the government to double money supply to solve the budget crisis, an idea both ministers and central bank officials reject out of hand because they say it would create hyper-inflation.

"When I saw the bill on new cash, my first thought was that an enemy country's agents had decided to finish off Russia's economy and suggested this plan," Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin told Interfax news agency.
"It is hard for me to imagine the consequences of such an injection of cash into the economy... We have never looked into an option of doubling monetary supply, even theoretically."
Parliament will discuss the bill, together with the government plan to cut spending, on May 21.

The International Monetary Fund, which is backing Russian economic reforms with a three-year $10 billion loan, is broadly satisfied with Russia's tough monetary policy, viewing it as Moscow's best guarantee against soaring inflation.
But they withheld or delayed several tranches of the loan over the last nine months, worried that Russia was not doing enough to crack the problem of tax evasion and low tax revenues.
Officials said last month that Russia received only 49 percent of planned tax receipts in the first quarter and only 16 percent of Russian companies paid taxes in full last year.
The IMF's board will meet on Friday and is expected to resume its lending programme to Russia this week after a gap of several months, offering almost $700 million of budget support.

The fund, confident that the overall thrust of economic policy meets its main demands, is monitoring Russia's economic performance once every three months, compared to the monthly monitoring carried out in previous years.
"Normally after board consideration Russia would become eligible to make the first drawing under the 1997 programme," IMF Moscow representative Martin Gilman said on Wednesday.
Ministers' next economic priority is forcing the spending cuts through parliament.
Kudrin said lower spending would help Russia shift to a new tax code, which provides for fewer taxes and a lower tax take.
"This corresponds to our strategic goal of cutting government spending and its part in GDP and gradually lowering the tax burden," he said.
Russia has also announced plans to tap securities markets for extra funds and to raise money by reclaiming debts owed to Moscow by other countries.
This hinges in part on Russia, a big debtor in its own right, joining the Paris Club of creditor states.

Paris Club chairman Christian Noyer said on Wednesday he hoped for an agreement in principle on Russia's entry to the creditor nations grouping by the G7 summit in Denver, next month but technical problems still had to be resolved.
Russia is owed billions of dollars by countries lent money by the Soviet Union and by former Soviet republics which owe money for energy supplies. ($ = 5757 Russian Roubles)
